referenceCard.title: Lists and dicts

subtitle: Many values under one name: in order (list) or by key (dict). And two names can share one.

teach.body: xs = [5, 8, 3] is a list. Positions start at 0: xs[0] is 5, xs[2] is 3, and xs[-1] counts from the end (3). len(xs) is 3, so the valid positions are 0 to len(xs) − 1; xs[3] stops with an IndexError. xs.append(4) adds to the end, changing the list in place. for x in xs: visits each item.
teach.title: Lists: in order, by position

teach.body:
ages = {"Ana": 30} maps keys to values. ages["Ana"] reads 30; ages["Bo"] = 25 adds or updates a key. Reading a key that isn't there stops with a KeyError, so ask first with "Bo" in ages, or read with a default: ages.get("Bo", 0). Counting pattern: d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1.

A related Python habit: and / or hand back one of their two values, not always True or False. name or "guest" gives name unless it's empty, so it's a quick default; 3 or 0 is 3 and 0 and 5 is 0.
teach.title: Dicts: by key

teach.body: b = a never copies anything, numbers included: both names label the same object. The difference is that lists and dicts can be changed in place (append, d[k] = v), and that change is visible through every name for them. a = a + 1 doesn't change a number; it moves a to a new one. Passing a list to a function works the same way: the parameter is another label on your list. a = something_new moves only a. For a separate copy, use a.copy().
teach.title: Two names, one list
